8.title: you've said it a thousand times
8.hook: you've said it a thousand times — at a table, at a funeral
8.howItsDone: Christians say amen at the end of prayers, hymns and blessings, usually all together, as a way of saying "yes, we agree" to what was just prayed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Bible. Your line was one story, many books. Week one is behind you. Week two opens with a short word, the one that ends so many prayers.

At the end of grace, right before anyone's allowed to eat. At a funeral, quietly, along with everyone else. Amen to that, as a joke. You've said it more times than you could count, and it's easy to hear it as the end: the prayer's over, you can open your eyes. It means something closer to the opposite.
screen: `AMEN.` → `YOU'VE SAID IT A THOUSAND TIMES.` → `IT DOESN'T MEAN THE END.`

segments.voice: Amen is Hebrew, from a root, aman, that means firm. Solid. The kind of thing you can put your weight on. The same root gives Hebrew its words for faithfulness and trust. So amen isn't a sign-off. It's yes. That's solid. So be it. It's old. In one scene in the books of Moses, a list of rules is read aloud to a whole people, and after each one: "And all the people shall answer and say, Amen." A room answering yes. Then a detail that's easy to miss. In the Gospels, Jesus puts the word in a strange place: at the start. The old English wording is "Verily, verily, I say unto you." Underneath verily is amen, amen. Usually amen came after, to agree with something already said. He said it first, vouching for his words before he spoke them. And the last book of the Bible goes further still. It calls him "the Amen, the faithful and true witness." Not just someone who says yes. The yes itself.
screen: `AMEN — FIRM. SOLID.` · `NOT GOODBYE. YES.` · `THE ROOM ANSWERS.` · `HE SAID IT FIRST.` · then, large: `THE YES ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Bring to mind one thing that's true and good in your life right now, something solid enough to put your weight on. Stay with it. Each time you breathe out, let the answer be yes. If you pray, you can let that yes be an amen.
Amen. Firm, truly, so be it: a yes, not a goodbye. Eighth word.
Your line: let it be so. Next time a room says it, you'll know what everyone is agreeing to. Day eight.

9.title: a gift you didn't earn
9.hook: a gift you didn't earn; your grandmother said it before dinner
9.tomorrow: a carpenter's son from a nowhere town, not a stained-glass window
9.howItsDone: Many Christians say grace, a short prayer of thanks, before meals, and churches speak of grace as God's free gift, received in faith and, for many, through sacraments like baptism and communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: amen, and your line was let it be so. Today, the prayer that comes right before so many of those amens.

The food is on the table, everybody's hungry, and somebody's grandmother says: wait. We haven't said grace. Heads go down. A few words, maybe the same ones she's said every night for years. Then amen, and the forks move. Saying grace meant saying thanks. But Christians use the word for something much larger: a gift you didn't earn.
screen: `WE HAVEN'T SAID GRACE.` → `NOT JUST THANKS.` → `A GIFT YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

segments.voice: The Greek word in the New Testament is charis: a gift, a favor, kindness given freely. It's where English gets charisma, a gift someone just has. And it hides inside a word from day one: Eucharist, thanksgiving. In Greek, the gift and the thank-you belong to one family. Now the part that cuts against the grain. So much of life runs on earning. You work, you get paid. You study, you pass. Grace doesn't work like that. One of Paul's letters says it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Not a wage. A gift. Paul also describes a problem he begged the Lord three times to take away. He never says what it was. The answer he says he got was this: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." Not the problem removed. Enough, given right inside it. Churches have long argued about how grace reaches a person: through the sacraments, through faith, through both. The word itself keeps its meaning: given, not earned. The grandmother at the table wasn't paying for dinner. She was saying: this came to us. Thank you.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and notice your breathing. You didn't make this breath. It just came, the way it's been coming all day while you weren't paying attention. Let each breath in be a gift you didn't earn. Let each breath out be a thank-you, said inside or not said at all.
Grace. Charis: a gift you didn't earn, freely given. Ninth word.
Your line: you are already held. That's what grace says, before anyone has earned anything. That's day nine.

10.title: a carpenter's son from a nowhere town, not a stained-glass window
10.hook: a carpenter's son from a nowhere town, not a stained-glass window
10.carry: he ate with the wrong people on purpose
10.tomorrow: the prayer a room says without a page
10.howItsDone: Christians come to know Jesus mainly through the four Gospels, read aloud in church services, and they pray to him or in his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grace, a gift you didn't earn. Today, the name at the center of everything on this path.

A stained-glass window, lit from behind. A painting with a golden circle around his head. A calm face on a card in a hospital waiting room. Those are the usual pictures of Jesus. Now try a different one. A man with rough hands, dust from his trade on his clothes. A family the neighbors knew by name. When he started to teach, the neighbors weren't impressed. They were confused. Isn't that just the builder?
screen: `NOT A STAINED-GLASS WINDOW.` → `ROUGH HANDS. A KNOWN FAMILY.` → `ISN'T THAT JUST THE BUILDER?`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Jesus is the English form of a Greek name, which comes from the Hebrew Yeshua, the same name as Joshua. It means, roughly, God saves. It wasn't a rare name; one of Paul's letters mentions another man called Jesus. Then the job. When he comes home to teach, the neighbors ask, in the old English: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The Greek word is tekton: a builder, a craftsman. It could mean wood, and it could mean stone. Either way, a working man with a trade. Then the town. Nazareth, in Galilee, a place nobody in the story expects much from. When one man first hears where Jesus is from, he says: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" His friend answers: "Come and see." But in Mark's Gospel, what gets people talking isn't where he came from. It's who he eats with. He sits down at the house of a tax collector, at a table full of people others avoided. Some religious teachers ask his followers how he can eat with tax collectors and sinners. He answers: healthy people don't need a doctor. Sick people do. The meal itself is the message. Christians say much more about Jesus: that he is the Son of God, that he died and rose again. The path gets to all of that. It starts at a table.
screen: `YESHUA — THE NAME JOSHUA.` · `TEKTON — A BUILDER.` · `NAZARETH — COME AND SEE.` · `A TABLE WITH THE WRONG PEOPLE.` · then, large: `IT STARTS AT A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and picture a table you've eaten at. Notice who usually sits there. Now picture one person who usually doesn't: someone you'd never think to invite. Give them a chair, just in your mind, and stay with the fuller table for a while. If you pray, you can bring them into it.
Jesus. Yeshua: God saves. A builder's name from a small town, at the center of the whole Christian path. Tenth word.
Your line: he ate with the wrong people on purpose. In the Gospels, that's what got him talked about. Day ten.

11.title: the prayer a room says without a page
11.hook: "Our Father": the family word, plain asks, and two endings
11.tomorrow: who your neighbor turns out to be
11.howItsDone: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer at home and in church, where the congregation often says it together, aloud. Some churches say "debts" and others "trespasses"; Catholics usually stop at "deliver us from evil" when praying it alone, while Protestant churches usually say it through "for thine is the kingdom" to the amen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jesus, the builder who ate with the wrong people on purpose. Today, the prayer he taught his friends.

Weddings, funerals, a locker room before a big game. Our Father, who art in heaven. A whole room can say it without anyone holding a page. Then, near the end, a small awkward moment. Some people stop at deliver us from evil. Others keep going: for thine is the kingdom. Nobody got it wrong. Here's why, and what the very first word is doing.
screen: `A PRAYER SAID BY HEART.` → `SOME STOP. SOME KEEP GOING.` → `NOBODY GOT IT WRONG.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the old English: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name." Start with Father. Jesus spoke Aramaic, and once, praying the night before he died, a Gospel keeps his own word: Abba. The family word, what a child says at home and a grown son still says to his dad. You may have heard it means daddy; scholars push back, since adults used it too. But it isn't a courtroom title. Then our. Not my. The whole prayer never once says I, me or my. Even said alone in a quiet room, it assumes a family around you. Then come the asks: that God's name be honored, that his kingdom come on earth as in heaven, bread for today, forgiveness as we forgive, and rescue from evil. One of those lines changes from church to church. Some say forgive us our debts, the older wording of the Gospel. Others say trespasses, from an old English prayer book. And the ending. The oldest copies of the Gospel stop at deliver us from evil. An early Christian handbook has a line of praise after it, and later copies carry the longer ending. So Catholics usually stop at evil, and at Mass the praise comes a moment later. Protestants usually say it straight through to the amen.
screen: `ABBA — THE FAMILY WORD.` · `OUR, NOT MY.` · `DEBTS OR TRESPASSES?` · `TWO ENDINGS, BOTH OLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Think of the word our, and let one person you love come to mind. Then widen it to the people you'll pass today, strangers included. If you pray, you can say the opening line slowly: Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. If you don't, rest in the word our, and everyone it takes in.
The Lord's Prayer. The family word, Abba, Father, then a few plain asks. Eleventh word.
Your line: you're not addressing a stranger. That's what the first word says. Day eleven, done.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO YOUR NEIGHBOR TURNS OUT TO BE.`

12.title: who your neighbor turns out to be
12.hook: a good Samaritan on the local news, and who the Samaritans actually were
12.carry: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you
12.howItsDone: Christians read the Good Samaritan as a picture of what loving your neighbor looks like in practice. Many churches, hospitals and charities are named after it, and many Christians take it as a reason to help strangers in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Lord's Prayer, which opens with our, not my. Today, a story Jesus told when someone asked where our ends.

A good Samaritan stops at a car crash, and it's on the local news. There are laws named after the phrase, and hospitals. Hardly anyone who uses it knows who the Samaritans were, or why, to the first people who heard it, a good Samaritan sounded almost like a contradiction. It starts with a man who knew his Bible very well. He and Jesus agree on the heart of it: love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself. Then the man asks the follow-up everybody quietly wants to ask. "And who is my neighbour?"
screen: `A GOOD SAMARITAN, ON THE NEWS.` → `WHO WERE THE SAMARITANS?` → `"AND WHO IS MY NEIGHBOUR?"`

segments.voice: Jesus answers with a story, in Luke's Gospel. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves." They strip him, beat him and leave him half dead in the ditch. A priest comes down the road, sees him, and passes by on the other side. Then a Levite, who served in the Temple, does the same. The story never says why. They're characters in a story, not a verdict on anyone's faith; Jesus and the man asking him were Jews too. Then a third traveler: a Samaritan. Samaritans and Judeans were related peoples who shared the books of Moses, but they worshipped on different mountains and had centuries of bad blood between them. So the hero of the story comes from across the line. And he's the one who stops. The old English says "he had compassion on him." He bandages the wounds, pours in oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays for his stay, with a promise to cover whatever else it costs. Then the twist. The man had asked: who counts? Jesus turns it around: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" Not who qualifies. Who acted like one. The man answers, "He that shewed mercy on him." And Jesus says: "Go, and do thou likewise."
screen: `A MAN IN THE DITCH.` · `TWO PASS BY.` · `THE ONE FROM ACROSS THE LINE STOPS.` · `NOT WHO QUALIFIES. WHO ACTED.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU LIKEWISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let a breath out. Think back over this week and find one moment when someone needed something and you passed by on the other side: a text you didn't answer, a coworker who looked lost. No need to judge yourself. Everyone passes by sometimes. Just see the moment clearly, and picture what stopping would have looked like. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer. If you don't, hold them in mind.
The Good Samaritan. The man from across the line who stopped, and turned the question from who counts to who acts. Twelfth word.
Your line: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you. Not who's close. Who's there. That's day twelve.

13.title: the father runs
13.hook: the father runs — old men didn't run
13.howItsDone: Christians read the Prodigal Son as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who returns. The Orthodox calendar names a Sunday before Lent after it, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching often connects it with confession and repentance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Good Samaritan, the man from across the line who stopped. Today, another story Jesus told, about a road home.

A grown son is walking up a dusty road toward the house he grew up in. He left badly. He took money that wasn't really his yet, and it's gone. Now he's broke, and he's practicing a speech in his head, the way you might rehearse a hard phone call. He isn't hoping to be forgiven. He's hoping to be hired. And while he's still far off, before he can say a word, he sees his father, an old man, running toward him.
screen: `A SON WHO LEFT BADLY.` → `A SPEECH, REHEARSED.` → `AN OLD MAN, RUNNING.`

segments.voice: It's in Luke's Gospel, and it's usually called the Prodigal Son. Prodigal isn't in the story. It's an old word for wasteful, and the name came later. A man has two sons. The younger asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is still alive; some readers hear in that: I wish you were already gone. The father gives it to him. The son goes off to a far country and spends every coin. Then a famine hits, and he ends up feeding pigs, hungry enough to envy what they eat. Then, in the old English, "when he came to himself," he rehearses his speech: I've sinned; make me one of your hired workers. Now the moment. "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Some scholars of the period say a dignified older man didn't run in public. The text only says he ran. Had compassion is the same Greek word Luke uses for yesterday's Samaritan: his gut turned over. The son starts the speech, and the father never lets him reach the part about being a servant. He calls for the best robe, a ring, shoes and a feast. "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." But the older brother, who stayed and worked, hears the party and won't go in. The father goes out to him too, and pleads. The story ends there. We never find out if he goes in.
screen: `HIS SHARE, NOW.` · `FEEDING PIGS, FAR FROM HOME.` · `THE FATHER RUNS.` · `THE OLDER BROTHER, OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `HE WAS LOST, AND IS FOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let a breath out. Think of a place, or a person, you've drifted from. Maybe you left badly. Maybe it just faded. Picture the road back. Now picture them seeing you from far off and coming toward you before you've said anything. Stay with that picture. If you pray, you can hold the father's words: he was lost, and is found. If you don't, just let the picture be.
The Prodigal Son. The one who wasted everything, and the father who ran to meet him anyway. Thirteenth word.
Your line: you can come home. Christians have long heard the father as a picture of God: running to the one who left, walking out to the one who stayed. Day thirteen.

14.title: "blessed are the poor in spirit"
14.hook: "blessed are the poor in spirit" — the upside-down list
14.tomorrow: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
14.howItsDone: Christians read the Beatitudes as a guide for daily life. In the Catholic calendar they're the Gospel reading on All Saints' Day, and in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy they're often sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prodigal Son, and a father running down the road. Your line was you can come home. Two weeks today.

Hashtag blessed. It turns up under the new car, the beach photo, the engagement ring. Now a hillside in Galilee. Crowds have followed a teacher out of the towns, many of them sick. He sits down and starts a long talk with a list of who's blessed. And every name on it is the one you wouldn't expect. The poor. The ones who are crying. The gentle ones who never win an argument. It opens what Christians call the Sermon on the Mount.
screen: `WHO GETS CALLED BLESSED?` → `A HILLSIDE. A CROWD.` → `EVERY NAME IS UNEXPECTED.`

segments.voice: They're called the Beatitudes, from the Latin word for blessed. In Matthew's Gospel they're usually counted as eight, and each has the same shape: blessed are these people, because this will happen to them. The first, in the old English: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The second: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." Then the meek, who will inherit the earth. The hungry for what's right. The merciful. The pure in heart. The peacemakers. And the people hounded for doing right. Then the word itself. The Greek word for blessed, makarioi, wasn't a churchy word. In ordinary Greek it described the fortunate, the happy. Old poets even used it for the gods, who had nothing to worry about. So the sentence lands like this: the lucky ones are the broke ones. The lucky ones are the ones at the funeral. It's meant to make you blink. Another Gospel has a shorter, blunter version: blessed are you poor, with no in spirit at all. Poor in money, poor in pride, or both: Christians have long talked about the difference. Either way, the list turns the ladder over. Later Jesus says it in a way that became a saying: "the last shall be first, and the first last."
screen: `EIGHT BLESSINGS, ONE SHAPE.` · `MAKARIOI — THE LUCKY ONES.` · `BLESSED ARE YOU POOR.` · `THE LADDER TURNED OVER.` · then, large: `THE LAST SHALL BE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and let one long breath out. Think of one person you tend to overlook. Not someone you dislike; someone you just don't see. The person who cleans the building. The quiet one in the group chat. Hold their face in your mind. If you pray, you can hold them there the way you would in a prayer. If you don't, just let them be first in your mind for a little while.
The Beatitudes. Eight blessings that start at the bottom. Fourteenth word. Amen, grace, Jesus, the Lord's Prayer, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Beatitudes: that's week two.
Your line: the last shall be first. Week three brings love, faith, songs that shout, a cross and an empty tomb. Day fourteen.

fork.reveal: "blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." the list starts at the bottom, and it stays there.

original.note: Greek. blessed, fortunate, happy. every Beatitude in Matthew opens with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: nice sayings for a greeting card.
what it means: an upside-down list — the people everyone overlooks are called fortunate first.
what a scholar hears: makarioi, a word Greek poets used for the carefree gods, pinned on the poor and the grieving. Latin said beati, and that gave English "beatitude."
